verses.zh: 我－保罗，就是与你们见面的时候是谦卑的，不在你们那里的时候向你们是勇敢的，如今亲自藉着基督的温柔、和平劝你们。
verses.en: Now I, Paul, appeal to you[NOTE:1] personally[NOTE:2] by the meekness and gentleness[NOTE:3] of Christ (I who am meek[NOTE:4] when present among[NOTE:5] you, but am full of courage[NOTE:6] toward you when away!)—
notes: The word “personally” is supplied to reflect the force of the Greek intensive pronoun αὐτός (autos) at the beginning of the verse.

Or “leniency and clemency.” D. Walker, “Paul’s Offer of Leniency of Christ (2 Corinthians 10:1): Populist Ideology and Rhetoric in a Pauline Letter Fragment (2 Cor 10:1-13:10)” (Ph.D. diss., University of Chicago, 1998), argues for this alternative translation for three main reasons: (1) When the two Greek nouns πραΰτης and ἐπιείκεια (prautēs and epieikeia) are used together, 90% of the time the nuance is “leniency and clemency.” (2) “Leniency and clemency” has a military connotation, which is precisely what appears in the following verses. (3) 2 Cor 10-13 speaks of Paul’s sparing use of his authority, which points to the nuance of “leniency and clemency.”
verses.commentary:
10:1 "Now I, Paul, myself urge you" Paul does not use the "we" of previous chapters
because he is defending himself personally from the accusations of the false teachers. Paul
used autos and ego (cf. 2 Cor. 12:13; Rom. 7:25; 9:3; 15:24; and in Gal. 5:2
egō and Paulos) to emphasize that this was his personal plea.

For "urge" see full note at 2 Cor. 1:4-11.

▣ "by the meekness and gentleness of Christ" Paul used the appropriate attitude
and methodologies even with these false teachers (cf. Matt. 11:29). Meekness was not seen as
a virtue by Greek thinkers (i.e., Socrates, Aristotle, Stoics). This reflects one of the faction's
criticisms of Paul. M. R. Vincent's Word Studies, vol. 2, asserts that in the Septuagint

- "meekness" (praus, 2 Cor. 10:1)

- "meek" (tapeinos, 2 Cor. 10:1)

- "poor" (penēs, v 9:9)

are used to translate the same Hebrew words. Remember, the NT was written by Hebrew/Aramaic
thinkers writing in Koine Greek. They contrast the rich and powerful vs. the lowly and down-trodden (p. 832).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT

▣ "who am meek when face to face with you, but bold toward you when absent" This
evaluation may refer to Paul's severe letter that was lost (cf. 2 Cor. 1:9-11).

Notice his play on the concept of "meekness."

- He calls Christ meek (i.e., praus, used of the Messiah in Matt. 21:5)

- believers in Matt. 5:5; 1 Pet. 3:4,15

- In this phrase he uses the SYNONYM tapeinos (cf. Louw and Nida, Greek-English Lexicon, vol. 1, p. 748),
which is also used of

- Jesus (cf. Matt. 11:29)

- Paul (cf. 2 Cor. 11:7; 12:21)

▣ "bold" See note at 2 Cor. 5:6.

verses.zh: 有人以为我是凭着血气行事，我也以为必须用勇敢待这等人；求你们不要叫我在你们那里的时候，有这样的勇敢。
verses.en: now I ask that when I am present I may not have to be bold with the confidence that (I expect) I will dare to use against some who consider us to be behaving[NOTE:1] according to human standards.[NOTE:2]
verses.commentary:
10:2 "I ask" This is the Greek term deomai, which means to ask with urgency or to
plead. It is synonymous to the term (i.e., parakaleō, cf. Louw and Nida, Greek-English
Lexicon, vol. 1, p. 408) Paul used it in 2 Cor. 10:1 (cf. 2 Cor. 2:8; 5:20; 6:1; 8:6; 9:5;
12:8,18; 13:11). He is urgently pleading with these believers to reevaluate what they have heard
from the false teachers.

▣ "that when I am present" Paul did not want to return to Corinth until things had
changed. He did not want to be bold, but gentle.

▣ "I need not be bold with the confidence with which I propose to be courageous
against some" In this context there is a play on the Greek word for "flesh." The false teachers were accusing
Paul of acting from the lowest, base human motives (i.e., in the flesh). While Paul admits that
he is in the flesh (i.e., physical body, cf. 2 Cor. 10:3), he strongly asserts that he is not
acting from fleshly motives (cf. 2 Cor. 1:17; 2:17; 4:3; 7:2; 10:3-4).

For "confidence" see note at 2 Cor. 3:4.

▣ "propose. . .regard" This is a play on the Greek word logizomai. Paul uses

- the VERB (PRESENT MIDDLE [deponent] INDICATIVE) to describe his thoughts

- the PARTICIPLE (PRESENT MIDDLE [deponent]) to describe the false teachers' false accusations.

- This may even have been a technical term from the Sophists (see Bruce W. Winter, Philo and Paul Among the Sophists).
See fuller note of the term at 2 Cor. 3:5.

▣ "walked" This is a Hebrew idiom for lifestyle behavior (e.g., Eph. 4:1,17; 5:2,1).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH. . .THE WAY

▣ "according to the flesh" They were judging Paul in light of their society's norms
(cf. 1 Cor. 9:8; 15:32; Rom. 3:5; Gal. 1:11; 3:15). Believers have a different standard—the
revealed word of God:

- Old Testament

- Christ

- New Testament

SPECIAL TOPIC: FLESH (sarx)

verses.zh: 因为我们虽然在血气中行事，却不凭着血气争战。
verses.en: For though we live[NOTE:1] as human beings,[NOTE:2] we do not wage war according to human standards,[NOTE:3]
verses.commentary:
10:3-6 Paul uses a series of military examples to describe the daily struggle between
the Christian and spiritual wickedness (cf. Rom. 7; 8:3-11). This spiritual wickedness is
defined in 2 Cor. 10:5 as human logic, wisdom, and argumentation against the gospel (cf. Eph. 6:10-18).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRITUAL WARFARE

10:3 Paul uses the term "flesh" in vv. 2-3 in very distinct ways.

- in a physical human body, vv. 2, 3a; 5:16

- in a manner characteristic of a fallen human person (i.e., worldly, self-seeking, v. 3b; assumed connotation
of 2 Cor. 1:17; 11:18; Phil. 3:4)

For a more detailed list see
SPECIAL TOPIC: FLESH (sarx)

▣ "war" This is the term strateuō, from which we get the English term
strategy. It was used of a soldier (cf. 1 Cor. 9:7; 2 Tim. 2:4) or as imagery for a spiritual
battle (cf. here and 1 Tim. 1:18). There is an ongoing conflict in the spiritual realm (cf. Eph. 3:2; 4:14; 6:10-20).

verses.zh: 我们争战的兵器本不是属血气的，乃是在　神面前有能力，可以攻破坚固的营垒，
verses.en: for the weapons of our warfare are not human weapons,[NOTE:1] but are made powerful by God[NOTE:2] for tearing down strongholds.[NOTE:3] We tear down arguments[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “are not fleshly [weapons].” The repetition of the word “warfare” does not occur in the Greek text, but is supplied for clarity.
Or “but (are) divinely powerful,” “but they have divine power,” or “but are powerful for God’s [service]”; Grk “but are powerful to God.”
Ultimately Paul is referring here to the false arguments of his opponents, calling them figuratively “strongholds.” This Greek word (ὀχύρωμα, ochurōma) is used only here in the NT.
verses.commentary:
10:4-5 There is a series of things in 2 Cor. 10:4-5 which Paul mentions as part of the spiritual conflict.

- destruction of fortresses (ochurōma)

- destruction of speculation (logizomai)

- destruction of every lofty thing (huphōma)

- taking captive every thought (noēma)

These phrases possibly refer to the Sophists' terms and rhetoric, which Paul had
depreciated in 1 Corinthians 1-4 (cf. Bruce W. Winter, Philo and Paul Among the Sophists,
pp. 180-202).

10:4 "the weapons of our warfare" Paul has alluded to this spiritual warfare earlier in
2 Cor. 6:7. The book of Romans was written from Corinth about this same time. He also mentions
this warfare in Rom. 6:13 and 13:12. Peter uses the verb form in 1 Pet. 4:1, where he encourages
believers to arm themselves in their fleshly struggles. This context has several military images. The
Christian life is an ongoing battle with the enemies of humanity (i.e., the world, Satan, and the Adamic
nature, cf. Eph. 2:2-3; James 4:1,4,7).

A good resource book in this area is Three Crucial Questions About Spiritual
Warfare by Clinton E. Arnold, published by Baker.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRITUAL WARFARE

▣ "for the destruction of fortresses" This may be an allusion to Prov. 21:22
(larger context 2 Cor. 10:13-31). There has been much discussion about the meaning of this
phrase among commentators, but it is obvious that 2 Cor. 10:5 is a description of what
spiritual fortresses Paul is referring to. It appears he is addressing the false theology
of the false teachers.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FALSE TEACHERS

verses.zh: 将各样的计谋，各样拦阻人认识　神的那些自高之事，一概攻破了，又将人所有的心意夺回，使他都顺服基督。
verses.en: and every arrogant obstacle[NOTE:1] that is raised up against the knowledge of God, and we take every thought captive to make it obey[NOTE:2] Christ.
notes: The phrase “every arrogant obstacle” could be translated simply “all arrogance” (so L&N 88.207).
Grk “to the obedience of Christ,” but since Χριστοῦ (Christou) is clearly an objective genitive here, it is better to translate “to make it obey Christ.”
verses.commentary:
10:5

NASB
"destroying speculations"

NKJV
"casting down arguments"

NRSV
"destroy arguments"

TEV
"pull down"

NJB
"It is ideas that we demolish"

REB
"demolish sophistries"

Peshitta
"casting down imaginations"

See note at 2 Cor. 3:5.

NASB
"and every lofty thing"

NKJV
"and every high thing"

NRSV
"and every proud obstacle"

TEV
"every proud obstacle"

NJB
"every presumptuous notion"

Peshitta
"and every false thing"

This is the word for "height" used in the sense of lofty, human thinking. This
reflects the false teachers' over-emphasis on

- knowledge and human reasoning (cf. 1 Cor. 1:18-25; Col. 2:8)

- legalism (cf. Col. 2:16-23)

▣ "taking every thought captive to the obedience of Christ" The VERB
is a compound of "spear" and "to capture in battle." These false teachers were capturing the
thought and minds of the Corinthian believers. Paul would have us

- "renew our minds" (cf. Rom. 12:2; Eph. 4:23)

- protect our minds (cf. Eph. 6:17; Phil. 4:7)

Salvation is free, but the Christian life is characterized by obedience (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP), service, worship (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: WORSHIP), and perseverance (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: PERSEVERANCE. These are covenant responsibilities. There is an ongoing spiritual conflict (cf. Romans 7; Eph. 6:10-19)!

Paul uses the word "thought" (noēma) often in 2 Corinthians
(cf. 2 Cor. 2:11; 3:14; 4:4; 11:3), but only one other time, in Phil. 4:7. The Corinthian
over-emphasis on knowledge may have been the reason for his recurrent use of the term.
The Analytical Greek Lexicon Revised, Harold K. Moulton, ed., lists several
connotations (p. 280).

- the mind, the understanding, intellect ‒ 2 Cor. 3:14; 4:4

- the heart, soul, affections, feelings, disposition ‒ 2 Cor. 11:3

- a conception of the mind, thought, purpose, device ‒ 2 Cor. 2:11; 10:5

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: GNOSTICISM

verses.zh: 并且我已经预备好了，等你们十分顺服的时候，要责罚那一切不顺服的人。
verses.en: We are also ready to punish every act of disobedience,[NOTE:1] whenever your obedience is complete.
verses.commentary:
10:6 Paul warns the false teachers and their followers that their day of reckoning is coming (i.e., his visit
to Corinth). They accused him of being weak, but they simply misunderstood his patience with them

- for Christ's sake

- for the corporate health of this church

Note how "obedience" and "disobedience" are contrasted in v. 5 vs. v. 6. The "warfare" (v. 4) is
related to the thoughts and actions of the members of the house churches of Corinth. Those who are disobedient to Paul's
gospel must be

- brought into "the obedience of Christ," v. 5

- or removed from the fellowship of the church

The gospel of Christ demands right thinking and right living (cf. Luke 6:46; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP).

verses.zh: 你们是看眼前的吗？倘若有人自信是属基督的，他要再想想，他如何属基督，我们也是如何属基督的。
verses.en: You are looking at outward appearances.[NOTE:1] If anyone is confident that he belongs to Christ, he should reflect on this again: Just as he himself belongs to Christ, so too do we.
notes: The phrase is close to a recognized idiom for judging based on outward appearances (L&N 30.120). Some translators see a distinction, however, and translate 2 Cor 10:7a as “Look at what is in front of your eyes,” that is, the obvious facts of the case (so NRSV).
verses.commentary:
10:7 "You are looking" In Greek the inflected form could be

- an IMPERATIVE (cf. NRSV, NJB)

- an INDICATIVE (cf. NASB, TEV, NIV)

- The NKJV and ASV translate it as a question.

The church at Corinth was analyzing and criticizing on a fleshly/worldly/physical
level instead of a gospel focus.

▣ "If" This is a FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE. There were some
in the house churches at Corinth who had deceived themselves as to their spiritual condition and standing (i.e., "is
confident," PERFECT ACTIVE INDICATIVE, cf. 1 Cor. 14:37). The deception was permanent
(i.e., PERFECT TENSE).

▣ "himself" Paul uses this term, eautou, twice in this verse. These false
teachers had deceived themselves. This is the hardest spiritual condition to reason with or to affect.
This is self imposed spiritual blindness (like the Jewish leaders in John 9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE UNPARDONABLE SIN

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SIN UNTO DEATH

▣ "that just as he is Christ's so also are we" The false teachers were claiming their
own spiritual authority and standing, but were denying Paul's.

verses.zh: 主赐给我们权柄，是要造就你们，并不是要败坏你们；我就是为这权柄稍微夸口，也不至于惭愧。
verses.en: For if I boast somewhat more about our authority that the Lord gave us[NOTE:1] for building you up and not for tearing you down, I will not be ashamed of doing so.[NOTE:2]
notes: The word “us” is not in the Greek text but is supplied. Indirect objects in Greek were often omitted when clear from the context, and must be supplied for the modern English reader.

Grk “I will not be put to shame,” “I will not be ashamed.” The words “of doing so” are supplied to clarify for the reader that Paul will not be ashamed of boasting somewhat more about the authority the Lord gave him (beginning of v. 8).
verses.commentary:
10:8 "if" This is a THIRD CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE, which implies potential,
even probable, action (cf. 2 Cor. 11:1-12:13).

▣ "boast" This term (i.e., kauchaomai and its other forms) is used so often
in Paul's Corinthian letters.

- kauchaomai (glory, boast, cf. 1 Cor. 1:29,31; 3:21; 4:7; 13:3; 2 Cor. 5:12;
7:14; 9:2; 10:8,13,15,16,17; 11:12,16,18,30; 12:1,5,6,9)

- kauchēma (cf. 1 Cor. 5:6; 9:15,16; 2 Cor. 1:14; 5:12; 9:3)

- kauchēsis (cf. 1 Cor. 15:31; 2 Cor. 1:12; 7:4,14; 8:24; 11:10,17)

See fuller note on use of the word at 2 Cor. 1:12.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BOASTING

▣ "about our authority, which the Lord gave" This refers to Paul's Damascus Road
experience (cf. Acts 9:15,16; Rom. 1:5; Gal. 2:9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: AUTHORITY (exousia)

▣ "for building you up and not for destroying you" Paul repeats this phrase in
2 Cor. 13:10. This is similar to the call of Isaiah (cf. Isaiah 6) and Jeremiah
(cf. Jeremiah 1), except they were called to do both! Paul uses the same VERB
(i.e., kathairesis), which he used in 2 Cor. 10:4 (twice) for destroying strongholds
of human reasoning. Paul is called to destroy some things and ideas, but not the church
itself. He is called to defend and protect the church (cf. 2 Cor. 10:9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: EDIFY

▣ "I will not be put to shame" Paul is going to defend himself because the false
teachers had made him the issue. He defends himself to defend

- the authority he had been given

- the gospel he preached

This may reflect the OT promises of God (cf. Rom. 9:33 and 10:11, quoting Isa. 28:16),
where those who trust in God will not be ashamed or disappointed. Paul knew in Whom he trusted!

Even if Paul had boasted too much (cf. NRSV, TEV) in his call and appointment, it
was still true and God would defend him! Those who reject Paul's authority are condemned
(cf. 1 Cor. 14:37-38).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHAME

verses.zh: 我说这话，免得你们以为我写信是要威吓你们；
verses.en: I do not want to seem as though I am trying to terrify you with my letters,
verses.commentary:
10:9 Paul's letters were to promote the factious house churches' repentance, not to bring condemnation
(cf. 2 Cor. 7:5-13a). But for the false teachers it was a different story (cf. 2 Cor. 10:8,11; 13:10).

verses.zh: 因为有人说：「他的信又沉重又厉害，及至见面，却是气貌不扬，言语粗俗的。」
verses.en: because some say, “His letters are weighty and forceful, but his physical presence is weak[NOTE:1] and his speech is of no account.”[NOTE:2]
verses.commentary:
10:10 "For they say" "They say" follows uncial manuscript B, the Latin Vulgate, and the Peshitta
(Syriac translation of the fifth century). Most other Greek manuscripts have "he," which may refer
to a ring leader of the false teachers (cf. 2 Cor. 10:7,11; 11:4). The UBS4 has "he" with
no mention of the other variant.

▣ "his personal presence is unimpressive" A second century tradition of Paul's
physical description comes from Thessalonica in part of a non-canonical book entitled Paul and Thecla. It
says that he was short, bald, bow-legged, had bushy eyebrows and protruding eyes. Paul was not
a physically attractive man (cf. Gal. 4:14). Some of these physical characteristics may be related
to his thorn in the flesh (cf. 2 Cor. 12:7), which I think was eye problems, probably related to
his "road to Damascus" blinding.

It is possible that this phrase, like the next one, refers to Paul's public speaking
skills, which were a major item of contention (cf. 1 Cor. 1:17). This phrase often was used of a
"stage presence" (cf. Bruce W. Winter, After Paul Left Corinth, p. 35).

▣ "and his speech contemptible" This is a PERFECT PASSIVE PARTICIPLE. This
is a strong Greek term (cf. 1 Cor. 1:28; 6:4; 16:11; Rom. 14:3,10). Paul was not
a polished public speaker (i.e., Greek rhetorical style, cf. 1 Cor. 1:17; 2 Cor. 11:6). Apollos
was the eloquent, rhetorically trained preacher from Alexandria. However, Paul claims that though
unskilled in rhetorical style (cf. 2 Cor. 11:6), his message and authority were from Christ.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SOPHISTS

verses.zh: 这等人当想，我们不在那里的时候，信上的言语如何，见面的时候，行事也必如何。
verses.en: Let such a person consider this: What we say[NOTE:1] by letters when we are absent, we also are in actions when we are present.
verses.commentary:
10:11 The false teacher(s) have accused Paul of having strong letters, but a weak personal
presentation. Paul affirms that the strength which they affirmed in his letters would be equaled
by the strength of his personal presence if he had to come personally and set things straight himself!

verses.zh: 因为我们不敢将自己和那自荐的人同列相比。他们用自己度量自己，用自己比较自己，乃是不通达的。
verses.en: For we would not dare to classify or compare ourselves with some of those who recommend themselves. But when they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves, they are without understanding.[NOTE:1]
verses.commentary:
10:12 "but when they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves" Paul
has alluded to human commendations in 2 Cor. 3:1 (cf. 2 Cor. 10:18); now he expands this to human
comparisons. Obviously these false teachers were comparing themselves to Paul in such a way as to
accentuate their position and depreciate his.

Paul knew from his study of the OT (cf. 1 Sam. 16:7; Prov. 21:2) how fruitless this
was. He was probably also familiar with Jesus' teaching about people who attempt to justify themselves
(cf. Luke 10:29; 16:15; 18:9,14).

There is a note of sarcasm in this verse as there is in 2 Cor. 10:1. Paul used
this literary form often in 1 Corinthians.

There is an obvious word play between the two AORIST ACTIVE INFINITIVES.

- egkrinai (en and krinō), judge as belonging to the same category

- sugkrinai (sun and krinō), judge by comparing

In codex Bezae (fifth century uncial MS) there is a phrase left out at the end of
2 Cor. 10:12 and the beginning of 2 Cor. 10:13. It seems that a scribe's eye moved from
"ou" of 2 Cor. 10:12 to "ouk" of 2 Cor. 10:13 and left out the intervening words
("do not understand. But we will not"). The UBS4 gives the phrase's inclusion
a "B" rating (almost certain).

SPECIAL TOPIC: TEXTUAL CRITICISM

▣ "they are without understanding This was quite a shocking statement.

- to Greek philosophers it would depreciate their claim to superior spiritual knowledge

- to Hebrew thinkers it would be an allusion to the animals

verses.zh: 我们不愿意分外夸口，只要照　神所量给我们的界限构到你们那里。
verses.en: But we will not boast beyond certain limits,[NOTE:1] but will confine our boasting[NOTE:2] according to the limits of the work to which God has appointed us,[NOTE:3] that reaches even as far as you.
notes: Or “boast excessively.” The phrase εἰς τὰ ἄμετρα (eis ta ametra) is an idiom; literally it means “into that which is not measured,” that is, a point on a scale that goes beyond what might be expected (L&N 78.27).
The words “will confine our boasting” are not in the Greek text, but the reference to boasting must be repeated from the previous clause to clarify for the modern reader what is being limited.
Grk “according to the measure of the rule which God has apportioned to us as a measure”; for the translation used in the text see L&N 37.100.
verses.commentary:
10:13 Paul is alluding to his divine call and mandate (i.e., his "road to Damascus" experience,
cf. Acts 9; 22:3-16; 26:9-18) to be an Apostle to the Gentiles. He was not comparing or commending,
but stating God's call.

God's call on him as special representative to the Gentiles surely included the church
at Corinth (cf. 2 Cor. 10:14-15).

▣ "the sphere which God apportioned to us" The NASB Study Bible (p. 1701) has a good
comment on this phrase:

"10:13 the sphere which God apportioned to us. The picture
Paul has in mind may be that of an athletic contest in which lanes are
marked out for the different runners. In that case 'sphere' should be
rendered 'lane' (also in 2 Cor. 10:15-16). In intruding themselves into
Corinth, the false apostles had crossed into Paul's lane, which was the
lane that God had marked out and that had brought him to the Corinthians
as their genuine apostle. He has no intention of invading the territory
marked out for others and claiming their work as his own, as these false
teachers were doing. Others understand the Greek word in question to refer
to an assigned sphere of authority."

verses.zh: 我们并非过了自己的界限，好像构不到你们那里；因为我们早到你们那里，传了基督的福音。
verses.en: For we were not overextending ourselves, as though we did not reach as far as you, because we were the first to reach as far as you with the gospel about Christ.[NOTE:1]
notes: Grk “with the gospel of Christ,” but since Χριστοῦ (Christou) is clearly an objective genitive here, it is better to translate “with the gospel about Christ.”
verses.commentary:
10:14 "For we are not overextending" This is another "huper" compound,
huperekteinō. Paul uses this PREPOSITION often, even
coining new words.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PAUL'S USE OF HUPER COMPOUNDS

▣ "we were the first to come even as far as you in the gospel of Christ" Paul was the
founder of the Corinthian church, yet the false teachers were trying to take credit (cf. 2 Cor. 10:18b).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE GOSPEL

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KERYGMA OF THE EARLY CHURCH

verses.zh: 我们不仗着别人所劳碌的，分外夸口；但指望你们信心增长的时候，所量给我们的界限，就可以因着你们更加开展，
verses.en: Nor do we boast beyond certain limits[NOTE:1] in the work[NOTE:2] done by others, but we hope[NOTE:3] that as your faith continues to grow, our work may be greatly expanded[NOTE:4] among you according to our limits,[NOTE:5]
notes: Or “boast excessively.” The phrase εἰς τὰ ἄμετρα (eis ta ametra) is an idiom; literally it means “into that which is not measured,” that is, a point on a scale that goes beyond what might be expected (L&N 78.27).
That is, Paul’s work might be greatly expanded within the area of activity assigned to him by God.
verses.commentary:
10:15 "not boasting beyond our measure. . .in other men's labors" The false teachers
were taking credit for the Corinthian church, which Paul established.

verses.zh: 得以将福音传到你们以外的地方；并不是在别人界限之内，藉着他现成的事夸口。
verses.en: so that we may preach the gospel in the regions that lie beyond you, and not boast of work already done in another person’s area.
verses.commentary:
10:16 "so as to preach the gospel even to the regions beyond you" This seems to refer to Paul's
desire to go to Rome and/or Spain (cf. Acts 19:21; Rom. 15:22ff). He wanted established churches to
help him both with a contribution for Jerusalem and to enable him to travel to the western
Mediterranean and establish more churches in areas that had no gospel witness .

For "beyond," this is another "huper" compound, (huperekeinē).

verses.zh: 但夸口的，当指着主夸口。
verses.en: But the one who boasts must boast in the Lord.[NOTE:1]
notes: The traditional translation (“let the one who boasts boast in the Lord”) can be understood as merely permissive by the English reader, but the Greek verb καυχάσθω (kauchasthō) is a third person imperative.sn A quotation from Jer 9:24 (also quoted in 1 Cor 1:31).
verses.commentary:
10:17 "he who boasts is to boast in the lord" This is a quote
from the Septuagint of Jer. 9:23-24. It is also quoted in 1 Cor. 1:31. All human boasting is folly.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- Chapters 10 through 13 form a literary unit where Paul defends himself against the
accusations of the false teachers. The false teachers had made Paul himself the crux
of the argument. Therefore, reluctantly, he defends himself on human grounds, using
their catch words and rhetorical style. His purpose ultimately was to defend the gospel.

- Some examples of the charges levied against Paul.

- He was condescending when face to face, but courageous in his letters, 2 Cor. 10:1,9,11.

- He was acting from the lowest human motives, 2 Cor. 10:2.

- His personal appearance was not pleasant and his rhetorical delivery was poor;
2 Cor. 10:2,10

- He preached simply for money, 2 Cor. 11:8,12; 12:16.

- Paul's enemies

- There seem to be three groups involved.

- a native Corinthian contingent (the factions of 1 Corinthians 1-4, probably from some house churches)

- a Jewish contingent from Palestine (similar to Judaizers, 2 Cor. 10-13).

- possibly a hybrid of both

- From 1 Corinthians there seem to be groups attacking him for and from opposite positions

- a legalistic group (asceticism)

- an antinomian group (libertines)

- Because Paul mentions several letters that he had written to the church at Corinth,
which apparently have not been preserved, there has been scholarly speculation
about 2 Corinthians being a composite of these lost letters. It is certainly true
that Paul's use of the EPISTOLARY AORIST in referring to his
different letters has caused confusion as well as the obvious different literary
units which make up 2 Corinthians, which often seem to be out of chronological
and rational arrangement. See fuller discussion in Introduction to 2 Corinthians.

It is surely possible that the disjunctions were caused by Paul writing
this letter over a period of time and that new information continued to arrive
after he had written a literary unit. The letter begins in a positive affirmation,
but then turns negative.

Personally, the possibility that some of Paul's letters were lost does not
bother me (possibly they contained information that the Spirit did not want to
become Scripture), but the proposed composite nature of 2 Corinthians, which has
no evidence in the Greek manuscript tradition nor church tradition, but is simply
the speculation of modern western scholars does bother me! We must not force ancient
eastern thinkers and writers into modern western literary categories.
